TSMC chip capacity is ‘fierce’ battleground for AI customers, amid record quarter
headlines.summary: TSMC had a record quarter, but it can't make chips for everyone as Nvidia, Apple, Broadcom and AMD fight for capacity.
headlines.article_text: Nvidia, Apple, Broadcom in 'fierce' battle to make chips at TSMC Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points TSMC makes the vast majority of the world's most advanced chips, but soaring AI demand has sparked fierce competition for manufacturing capacity. Chip companies are cultivating relationships in Taiwan and making the case that they could become TSMC's next big customer. At the center of the competition is TSMC executive Kevin Zhang, who one customer describes as "the most popular person on the planet." In this article TSM Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 13:36 13:36 TSMC can't make chips for everyone, and competition is 'extremely fierce' Tech As Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.'s record quarter makes clear, demand from chipmakers shows no sign of slowing down. In fact, TSMC can't manufacture quickly enough. The artificial intelligence boom has created unending need for space on factory lines at the world's leading chip manufacturer, and it could put a chokehold on the entire industry's ability to scale. Last year, TSMC said it had the capacity to make more than 17 million 12-inch equivalent wafers. But customers want more. "The competition is extremely fierce," said Jordan Klein, an analyst at Mizuho Securities. "It's a game of who can get the most leverage and supply." TSMC makes the vast majority of the world's most advanced semiconductors, the graphics processors and central processors from Nvidia , AMD and Broadcom that are necessary for running AI workloads. Now a growing number of tech firms – Apple , Google , Amazon , Microsoft , Meta and OpenAI – also rely on TSMC to make custom in-house AI accelerators. TSMC North American CEO Sajiv Dalal told CNBC he gets at least 10 calls a day about wafer capacity. TSMC posted record profit for a sixth straight quarter on Thursday and expects fourth-quarter revenue to be 58% higher than a year earlier, driven by strong demand for its advanced chipmaking technologies. If compute demand continues to grow at the current rate over the next 12 to 18 months, Klein said capacity constraints at TSMC could threaten some of the industry's massive infrastructure investments and the "aggressive revenue growth targets" from the AI companies. U.S. hyperscalers are projecting well over $700 billion in capital expenditures this year, and analysts expect that figure to jump in 2027. AI ambitions are also threatened by a global shortage of memory chips. The logic chips that TSMC manufactures are more complex and expensive to produce. That means GPU and CPU leaders like Nvidia and AMD work out lengthy contracts and bespoke deals with TSMC behind closed doors years in advance. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and AMD CEO Lisa Su have both visited Taiwan multiple times this year. watch now VIDEO 3:33 03:33 This Nvidia challenger says its AI chip is 10x faster than a GPU Tech Sid Sheth, CEO of AI chip startup D-Matrix, has fostered a relationship with TSMC for more than 20 years, and his company relies on TSMC to manufacture its processors. Sheth said that for TSMC customers, many roads lead to Kevin Zhang, a senior vice president of the Taiwanese company and a central figure in determining which chipmakers get access to its coveted factory lines. He's "currently probably the most popular person on the planet," Sheth said in an interview. Sheth said that Jerry Qubain, D-Matrix's vice president of manufacturing, has been visiting TSMC since 1992 and goes to Taiwan three to four times a year. "This was even before Nvidia was founded," Sheth said. "That's a good example of a person we brought on board because of the relationships he has at TSMC." Qubain joined D-Matrix in 2024. TSMC declined to participate in this story. Betting on startups TSMC had 534 customers in 2025. While it doesn't name or rank them, its top 10 customers accounted for 78% of net revenue , with its top two bringing in 19% and 17%, respectively. That leaves startups competing for capacity against customers with far bigger orders. Sheth said TSMC is "selective," but has an incentive to back promising newcomers. "They were very supportive of Nvidia and Broadcom when they were very young companies, and now these are their biggest customers today," Sheth said. "They want to see a repeat of that." TSMC is hustling to bring much more capacity online, with new fabs in Taiwan, Japan and Arizona — it's making advanced chips in the U.S. for the first time. In July, TSMC announced it was adding $100 billion and "several more" fabs to the six planned in Arizona, bringing its total commitment to $265 billion. TSMC is also reportedly considering an entirely new fab location in Texas. watch now VIDEO 16:25 16:25 Inside TSMC's new chip fab where Apple will make chips in the U.S. Tech All of this will take years to come online. In the meantime, analysts say TSMC is adding tools like ASML's extreme ultraviolet lithography machines to existing factories to ramp up capacity. ASML smashed profit expectations in its earnings report Wednesday and said customers are interested in placing orders through 2030. TSMC isn't the only option. Capacity constraints create an opening for the other two leading advanced chip manufacturers, Samsung and Intel , to win customers. "People want a second source to be able to twist TSMC's arm and keep them honest on pricing," Dan Hutcheson, an analyst at TechInsights, told CNBC. That second source might be Intel, the only U.S.-based advanced logic manufacturer. Although its foundry business has been struggling with delays and setbacks for years, Hutcheson says all the big chipmakers are now testing there. Trade association SEMI expects 102 new chip fabs will come online globally by 2029, including 15 in the U.S. and 78 in Asia. China is the primary growth engine, expected to nearly triple capacity by 2030. In a race to catch up, American fab investments are projected to more than double by 2029. With an increasing Arizona presence and "extremely fierce" competition for wafer capacity, Klein says TSMC is "one of the best strategically positioned companies on the face of the planet." headlines.article_text: Southwest Airlines overhauls Rapid Rewards program Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Southwest Airlines is replacing its two tiers of elite frequent flyer status with silver, gold and platinum levels, similar to other carriers. The carrier will scrap its current status tiers, A-List and A-List Preferred, on Jan. 1. Southwest is also adding perks along the way to status tiers and changing requirements to earn Companion Pass. In this article LUV Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT A Southwest Airlines Boeing 737 airplane departs from San Diego International Airport on May 27, 2026. Kevin Carter | Getty Images News | Getty Images Goodbye, A-List and A-List Preferred. Southwest Airlines is scrapping its two-tier loyalty program starting next year and instead rolling out silver, gold and platinum levels that are similar to what other carriers offer, as the once-quirky airline seeks to increase revenue and reward its biggest spenders. Southwest executives have been overhauling the airline, getting rid of longtime customer perks like two free checked bags and open seating . It's now charging for some of those options, like rivals have been doing for years. Along with the shift from two to three loyalty levels, the carrier is also changing the names of its tiers. Under the old version, travelers could be classified into A-List or A-List Preferred, which was the higher level. "If you think about A-List and A-List Preferred, we don't even have [boarding] groups A, B and C anymore," Tony Roach, Southwest chief customer and brand officer, said in an interview. "So it was time to do a refresh to somewhat incorporate all the changes to seating and all these new experiences that we've been adding." Here's what's changing for the loyalty program: A-List and A-List Preferred Rapid Rewards status levels will go away on Jan. 1. A-List customers will be shifted to Silver status in the Rapid Rewards program. A-List Preferred members will get Gold status. A new Platinum tier will be added for the airline's "most engaged" customers. Customers can earn 1 Tier Qualifying Point, or TQP, per $1 spent on Southwest co-branded credit cards with Chase . Here are the new status requirements: Silver status will require 35,000 TQPs or 25 qualifying flights. Previously, A-List was 35,000 points or 20 flights. For Silver members, the points-earning bonus on flights will go up from 25% to 40%. To earn Gold , customers will have to reach 65,000 TQPs, down from 70,000 points for A-List Preferred, or take 50 flights. The points-earning bonus for those with that status goes from 100%, or double points earning, to 60% on qualifying flights. The new, top-tier Platinum status requires 140,000 TQPs or 100 qualifying flights. Platinum members will get a 120% earnings bonus on qualifying flights.
